entries.title: Fragrance (Parfum)
entries.why: Umbrella term for scent mixtures used to give products a smell. Formulas can include undeclared allergens and are often not fully disclosed as individual chemicals. A common trigger for contact dermatitis in sensitive people; EU rules require labelling of certain fragrance allergens above thresholds.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — fragrance allergen labelling
SCCS opinions on fragrance allergens (public summaries)

entries.title: Methylisothiazolinone (MIT)
entries.why: Preservative linked to a sharp rise in contact allergy. Leave-on cosmetics face EU restrictions; rinse-off products have concentration limits. Worth noticing on older or imported products that may predate stricter rules.
sources: EU CosIng / Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — isothiazolinone restrictions
SCCS opinions on methylisothiazolinone (public summaries)

entries.title: Methylchloroisothiazolinone (MCI)
entries.why: Preservative often used with MIT (MCI/MIT mix). Strong contact allergen; EU rules restrict leave-on use and limit rinse-off concentrations. Flag if you have reactive skin or a history of isothiazolinone allergy.
sources: EU CosIng / Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — isothiazolinone restrictions
SCCS opinions on MCI/MIT (public summaries)

entries.title: Butylparaben
entries.why: Preservative in the paraben family. Longer-chain parabens face more EU scrutiny for endocrine activity; SCCS has set maximum concentration limits for certain uses. Prefer products that avoid higher-concern parabens if that matters to you.
sources: SCCS opinions on parabens (public summaries)
EU CosIng entries and concentration restrictions (public)

entries.title: Propylparaben
entries.why: Common preservative; longer-chain parabens have faced greater regulatory scrutiny than methyl/ethyl parabens. EU SCCS opinions address concentration limits for certain applications—check labels if you prefer to minimise these.
sources: SCCS opinions on parabens (public summaries)
EU CosIng entries and concentration restrictions (public)

entries.title: BHA (Butylated hydroxyanisole)
entries.why: Antioxidant used to slow rancidity in oils and cosmetics. Classified as a possible human carcinogen by some agencies in other contexts; cosmetic use is permitted within limits. Included as a moderate concern for people who prefer to avoid it.
sources: EU CosIng entry for BHA (public)
IARC classification summaries (public) — context for other exposures

entries.title: BHT (Butylated hydroxytoluene)
entries.why: Antioxidant preservative for oils and fragrances. Generally considered lower concern than BHA at cosmetic use levels, but still debated by some consumers. Function is product stability, not skin treatment.
sources: EU CosIng entry for BHT (public)
EFSA/SCCS public evaluations of BHT where available

entries.title: DMDM hydantoin
entries.why: Preservative that slowly releases small amounts of formaldehyde to control microbes. Helpful for product safety against contamination, but a concern for people sensitive to formaldehyde or formaldehyde releasers.
sources: EU CosIng entry for DMDM hydantoin (public)
SCCS opinions on formaldehyde and releasers (public summaries)

entries.title: Quaternium-15
entries.why: Formaldehyde-releasing preservative formerly common in leave-on and rinse-off products. Associated with contact allergy; regulatory status has tightened in several markets. Worth avoiding if you react to formaldehyde releasers.
sources: EU CosIng / Cosmetic Regulation entries (public)
SCCS formaldehyde-releaser opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Imidazolidinyl urea
entries.why: Antimicrobial preservative that can release formaldehyde. Used to keep water-based formulas safe from spoilage; may bother people with formaldehyde sensitivity or reactive skin.
sources: EU CosIng entry for imidazolidinyl urea (public)
SCCS opinions on formaldehyde releasers (public summaries)

entries.title: Diazolidinyl urea
entries.why: Formaldehyde-releasing preservative related to imidazolidinyl urea. Effective against bacteria in creams and lotions; a contact-allergy concern for formaldehyde-sensitive users.
sources: EU CosIng entry for diazolidinyl urea (public)
SCCS opinions on formaldehyde releasers (public summaries)

entries.title: Homosalate
entries.why: UV filter used in sunscreens and day products. Under EU endocrine-disruption review with SCCS concentration opinions; still widely used within authorised limits. Flagged so you can notice high placement on the label if that concerns you.
sources: SCCS opinion on homosalate (public summary)
EU CosIng / Cosmetic Regulation UV-filter annexes (public)

entries.title: Octocrylene
entries.why: Common UV filter and photostabiliser for other filters. Subject to EU safety reassessments and public debate about degradation products; authorised within concentration limits. Function is sun protection, not a fragrance.
sources: SCCS opinion on octocrylene (public summary)
EU CosIng / Cosmetic Regulation UV-filter annexes (public)

entries.title: Benzophenone-3 (Oxybenzone)
entries.why: UV filter with greater public and regulatory scrutiny than many others, including EU concentration limits and endocrine-related assessments. Effective sun protection ingredient; some people prefer mineral filters instead.
sources: SCCS opinions on benzophenone-3 / oxybenzone (public summaries)
EU CosIng concentration restrictions (public)

entries.title: Triclosan
entries.why: Antimicrobial agent restricted in many cosmetic product types in the EU after safety reviews. Not needed for most everyday personal care; flagged when present as a higher-priority label item.
sources: EU CosIng / Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — triclosan restrictions
SCCS opinions on triclosan (public summaries)

entries.title: CI 20285 (coal-tar related dye)
entries.why: Colourant in the azo / coal-tar dye family subject to EU cosmetic use restrictions or purity requirements depending on product type. Colour is cosmetic only; some related dyes have tighter rules than everyday pigments.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation colourant annexes (public)
EU CosIng colourant entries (public)

entries.title: CI 26100 (Solvent Red 23)
entries.why: Red colourant with EU restrictions for certain cosmetic uses (e.g. limits around mucous membranes). Included so restricted coal-tar–related dyes surface in scoring when listed.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation colourant annexes (public)
EU CosIng entry for CI 26100 (public)

entries.title: Phenoxyethanol
entries.why: Widely used preservative that replaced some parabens and formaldehyde releasers. Generally considered low concern at typical cosmetic levels; rare irritation or allergy is possible. Function is keeping products microbially safe.
sources: SCCS opinion on phenoxyethanol (public summary)
EU CosIng entry for phenoxyethanol (public)

entries.title: Limonene
entries.why: Citrus-scented terpene and EU-listed fragrance allergen. Common in fragranced products and essential-oil blends; can oxidise on air exposure and contribute to contact allergy in sensitive people. Mild note only unless you know you react.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Linalool
entries.why: Floral/lavender-scented terpene and EU-listed fragrance allergen. Appears from essential oils and synthetic fragrance; oxidised forms are more sensitising. Low severity for most users; relevant if you avoid fragrance allergens.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Citronellol
entries.why: Rose-scented fragrance ingredient and EU-listed allergen. Used for scent rather than skincare benefit; may contribute to fragrance contact allergy when above labelling thresholds.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
IFRA standards context (public summaries)

entries.title: Geraniol
entries.why: Rose-like fragrance alcohol and EU-listed allergen. Present in many essential oils and perfume mixes; a mild sensitisation note for fragrance-sensitive users.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Eugenol
entries.why: Clove-scented phenol and EU-listed fragrance allergen. Can sensitise some users, especially at higher fragrance loads; also found in certain essential oils.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Coumarin
entries.why: Sweet hay-like fragrance note and EU-listed allergen. Used for scent; mild concern mainly for people with known fragrance allergy.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Cinnamal
entries.why: Cinnamon-scented aldehyde and relatively potent EU-listed fragrance allergen. More often a problem for fragrance-sensitive skin than mild terpenes; still a scenting agent, not a treatment.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Isoeugenol
entries.why: Fragrance allergen related to eugenol, often from spice or floral notes. Known sensitiser; EU labelling applies above thresholds. Mild–moderate note depending on your fragrance history.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Oakmoss (Evernia prunastri)
entries.why: Natural moss extract used in chypre and woody fragrances; well-known contact allergen with IFRA restrictions. Listed among classic fragrance sensitisers—relevant if oakmoss or perfume allergy is a concern.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
IFRA standards on oakmoss/tree moss (public summaries)

entries.title: Sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS)
entries.why: Strong foaming cleanser/surfactant. Not a banned or endocrine concern; can dry or irritate skin and scalp, especially at high concentration or with frequent use. Mild severity for irritation nuance only.
sources: EU CosIng entry for sodium lauryl sulfate (public)
SCCS/public reviews of alkyl sulfates as irritants (summaries)

entries.title: Retinol
entries.why: Vitamin A derivative used for anti-ageing and skin renewal. SCCS 2023 opinions address concentration limits and cumulative vitamin A exposure; can irritate and is not for everyone (e.g. pregnancy caution per product labelling). Low–moderate severity for informed use.
sources: SCCS opinion on vitamin A (retinol, retinyl esters) 2023 (public summary)
EU CosIng / Cosmetic Regulation entries (public)

entries.title: Talc
entries.why: Soft mineral powder used for texture and absorbency. Cosmetic talc should be asbestos-free under modern standards; historical contamination debates and inhalation concerns for loose powders drive a cautious low severity flag—not an automatic ban signal.
sources: EU CosIng entry for talc (public)
Public regulatory purity/asbestos requirements for cosmetic talc

entries.title: Aluminum salts (antiperspirant)
entries.why: Active antiperspirant salts that reduce sweat. Extensive use history; public debate about systemic aluminum is not matched by a cosmetic ban. Balanced low severity—function is sweat control; rinse-off and topical use differ from other aluminum exposures.
sources: SCCS opinions on aluminum in cosmetics (public summaries)
EU CosIng entries for aluminum chlorohydrate and related salts

entries.title: Cyclotetrasiloxane (D4)
entries.why: Cyclic silicone used for silky feel and spread. EU restricts D4 in rinse-off products largely on environmental (persistence/bioaccumulation) grounds rather than acute human toxicity. Framing is regulatory/environmental, not a medical claim.
sources: EU REACH / Cosmetic Regulation restrictions on D4 in rinse-off (public)
ECHA substance information on D4 (public summaries)

entries.title: Cyclopentasiloxane (D5)
entries.why: Very common cyclic silicone for slip and volatility. EU rinse-off restrictions focus on environmental profile (PBT-related concerns), not a claim that skin contact is acutely hazardous at cosmetic levels.
sources: EU REACH / Cosmetic Regulation restrictions on D5 in rinse-off (public)
ECHA substance information on D5 (public summaries)

entries.title: Benzyl alcohol
entries.why: Used as preservative, solvent, and fragrance component; also an EU-listed fragrance allergen above thresholds. Generally low concern at permitted levels; mild note for fragrance-sensitive users.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS opinions on benzyl alcohol where applicable (public)

entries.title: Hexyl cinnamal
entries.why: Jasmine-like fragrance allergen on the EU labelling list. Scenting agent only; low severity unless you avoid listed fragrance allergens.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Citral
entries.why: Lemon-scented terpene aldehyde and EU-listed fragrance allergen. Common in citrus oils and synthetic fragrance; can contribute to contact allergy above labelling thresholds. Mild note for fragrance-sensitive users.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Farnesol
entries.why: Floral fragrance alcohol and EU-listed allergen, also used as a mild antimicrobial scent component. Function is mainly scent; low severity unless you avoid listed fragrance allergens.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Benzyl salicylate
entries.why: Floral fragrance ester and EU-listed allergen. Used for scent and mild UV-absorbing character in perfume blends; mild contact-allergy note for sensitive users.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Benzyl benzoate
entries.why: Fragrance solvent and fixative, also an EU-listed fragrance allergen. Common in perfume bases; low severity for most users, relevant if you track fragrance allergens.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
EU CosIng entry for benzyl benzoate (public)

entries.title: Benzyl cinnamate
entries.why: Balsamic fragrance ester and EU-listed allergen. Scenting agent only; mild note for people who react to fragrance or cinnamon-family notes.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Cinnamyl alcohol
entries.why: Cinnamon-family fragrance alcohol and relatively well-known EU-listed allergen. Can sensitise fragrance-reactive skin more often than mild terpenes; still used only for scent.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Amyl cinnamal
entries.why: Floral-jasmine type fragrance aldehyde and EU-listed allergen. Common synthetic scent ingredient; mild severity unless you avoid labelled fragrance allergens.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Amylcinnamyl alcohol
entries.why: Fragrance alcohol related to amyl cinnamal and EU-listed allergen. Used for scent; low severity for general users, relevant for fragrance-sensitive skin.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Hydroxycitronellal
entries.why: Lily-of-the-valley type fragrance ingredient and established EU-listed allergen. Among the more frequently positive fragrance markers in patch testing; still a scent agent, not a treatment.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Alpha-isomethyl ionone
entries.why: Violet-scented ionone fragrance and EU-listed allergen. Common in floral perfume blends; mild contact-allergy note above labelling thresholds.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Anise alcohol
entries.why: Sweet anise-scented fragrance alcohol and EU-listed allergen. Used for scent; low severity for most people, flagged for fragrance-allergen awareness.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
SCCS fragrance allergen opinions (public summaries)

entries.title: Methyl 2-octynoate
entries.why: Green/violet-type fragrance ester and EU-listed allergen with a history of strong sensitisation potential at higher levels. Now used carefully under fragrance standards; still a meaningful allergen label item.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
IFRA standards context (public summaries)

entries.title: Treemoss (Evernia furfuracea)
entries.why: Natural moss extract used in woody/chypre fragrances; classic contact allergen related to oakmoss, with IFRA restrictions. Relevant if moss or perfume allergy is a concern.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — fragrance allergens
IFRA standards on oakmoss/tree moss (public summaries)

entries.title: Butylphenyl methylpropional (Lilial)
entries.why: Synthetic lily fragrance formerly common in leave-on and rinse-off products. Banned in EU cosmetics from March 2022 as a CMR substance (reproductive toxicity classification). Presence indicates a non-compliant or pre-ban/imported product.
sources: EU Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1902 — CMR ban including butylphenyl methylpropional (2021/2022)
EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — Annex II prohibited substances

entries.title: Hydroxyisohexyl 3-cyclohexene carboxaldehyde (Lyral/HICC)
entries.why: Floral fragrance allergen banned in EU cosmetics (phased ban completed 2021) after high rates of contact allergy. Strong sensitiser; should not appear in compliant EU-market products.
sources: EU Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1410 — ban of HICC (Lyral) in cosmetics
SCCS opinions on hydroxyisohexyl 3-cyclohexene carboxaldehyde (public summaries)

entries.title: Zinc pyrithione
entries.why: Antifungal/anti-dandruff agent formerly allowed in rinse-off hair products within limits. Banned in EU cosmetics from March 2022 following CMR classification. Presence indicates non-compliant or legacy product.
sources: EU Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1902 — CMR ban including zinc pyrithione (2021/2022)
EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — Annex II prohibited substances

entries.title: Hydroquinone
entries.why: Skin-lightening agent prohibited in EU cosmetics (Annex II), with only narrow professional-use exceptions historically for artificial nail systems. Not allowed as a general skin-bleaching cosmetic ingredient in the EU.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — Annex II (hydroquinone prohibited)
EU CosIng entry for hydroquinone (public)

entries.title: Lead acetate
entries.why: Lead salt formerly used in progressive hair dyes. Lead compounds are prohibited in EU cosmetics under Annex II; lead acetate must not appear in compliant products.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — Annex II (lead and its compounds prohibited)
EU CosIng / heavy metal prohibitions (public)

entries.title: Mercury compounds
entries.why: Mercury and most mercury compounds are prohibited in EU cosmetics (Annex II), including historical skin-lightening and preservative uses. Highly toxic; presence signals a banned or illegal product.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — Annex II (mercury and its compounds)
Minamata Convention context / public regulatory bans on mercury cosmetics

entries.title: Dibutyl phthalate (DBP)
entries.why: Plasticiser once common in nail polish for flexibility. Banned in EU cosmetics as a CMR substance (reproductive toxicity). Should not appear on compliant EU-market beauty products.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — Annex II (dibutyl phthalate prohibited)
EU CMR classifications for dibutyl phthalate (public)

entries.title: Benzisothiazolinone (BIT)
entries.why: Isothiazolinone preservative related to MIT/MCI, more often used in rinse-off and household products than leave-on cosmetics. Contact allergen; EU cosmetic use is tightly limited compared with industrial applications.
sources: EU CosIng / Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — isothiazolinone context
SCCS opinions on isothiazolinones (public summaries)

entries.title: Bronopol
entries.why: Antimicrobial preservative that can release small amounts of formaldehyde and form nitrosamines under some conditions. Useful against bacteria; a concern for formaldehyde-sensitive users and nitrosamine control.
sources: EU CosIng entry for bronopol (public)
SCCS opinions on formaldehyde and releasers (public summaries)

entries.title: Sodium hydroxymethylglycinate
entries.why: Preservative that can release formaldehyde to control microbes in water-based formulas. Milder public profile than some older releasers, but still relevant for people avoiding formaldehyde donors.
sources: EU CosIng entry for sodium hydroxymethylglycinate (public)
SCCS opinions on formaldehyde releasers (public summaries)

entries.title: Formaldehyde
entries.why: Biocide and known contact allergen with CMR classification. Free formaldehyde as an intentional cosmetic ingredient is heavily restricted/banned in modern EU rules; also released by some preservatives. High severity when listed as such.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — formaldehyde restrictions/Annex entries
SCCS opinions on formaldehyde and formaldehyde releasers (public summaries)
IARC monographs — formaldehyde (public classification summaries)

entries.title: Triclocarban
entries.why: Antimicrobial agent used historically in soaps and deodorants. Faces regulatory scrutiny and use limits similar in spirit to triclosan concerns; not needed for most everyday personal care.
sources: EU CosIng / Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — triclocarban restrictions (public)
SCCS opinions on triclocarban where available (public summaries)

entries.title: p-Phenylenediamine (PPD)
entries.why: Primary intermediate in permanent oxidative hair dyes and a well-known strong contact allergen. EU Annex III sets maximum concentrations and labelling (e.g. allergy warning). High-priority label item for hair-dye users.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — hair dye intermediates
SCCS opinions on p-phenylenediamine (public summaries)

entries.title: Toluene-2,5-diamine
entries.why: Oxidative hair-dye intermediate related to PPD, used in permanent colourants. Contact allergen with EU Annex III concentration limits and mandatory warnings. Flag if you have dye allergy history.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — hair dye intermediates
SCCS opinions on toluene-2,5-diamine (public summaries)

entries.title: Resorcinol
entries.why: Coupler/oxidant helper in permanent hair dyes and occasional use in other cosmetics. EU Annex III limits concentrations; can irritate and is under endocrine-related scientific discussion. Function is dye chemistry, not skincare benefit.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — resorcinol
SCCS opinions on resorcinol (public summaries)

entries.title: Ammonium persulfate
entries.why: Strong oxidiser used in hair bleaches and lighteners. Can cause contact dermatitis, respiratory sensitisation in salon settings, and irritation. Professional-use chemistry—high caution on consumer labels.
sources: EU CosIng entry for ammonium persulfate (public)
SCCS / occupational allergy literature summaries on persulfates (public)

entries.title: Cocamide DEA
entries.why: Coconut-derived foam booster and thickener in shampoos and cleansers. IARC classifies coconut oil diethanolamine condensate as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B); also linked to nitrosamine formation concerns with certain impurities. Moderate severity.
sources: IARC Monographs — coconut oil diethanolamine condensate (Group 2B summaries)
EU CosIng entry for cocamide DEA (public)

entries.title: Musk xylene
entries.why: Nitro musk fragrance with environmental persistence and EU restrictions/phase-outs under cosmetics and chemicals law. Rare in modern formulas; high concern if still listed.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation / REACH restrictions on musk xylene (public)
ECHA substance information on musk xylene (public summaries)

entries.title: Benzophenone
entries.why: UV absorber and fragrance component related to the benzophenone filter family. Under scientific and regulatory scrutiny (including impurity/degradation and classification discussions); distinct from benzophenone-3 but same chemical family.
sources: EU CosIng entry for benzophenone (public)
IARC/SCCS context for benzophenones where available (public summaries)

entries.title: Octinoxate (EHMC)
entries.why: Common chemical UVB filter (INCI: Ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate). Authorised within EU concentration limits; subject to public debate and endocrine-related research. Function is sun protection; mineral filters are an alternative preference for some users.
sources: EU CosIng / Cosmetic Regulation UV-filter annexes — ethylhexyl methoxycinnamate
SCCS opinions on UV filters (public summaries)

entries.title: 4-Methylbenzylidene camphor (4-MBC)
entries.why: Chemical UV filter with notable EU endocrine-disruption scrutiny and tightening regulatory status. Higher concern UV filter than many everyday filters; check current authorised use if listed.
sources: SCCS opinions on 4-methylbenzylidene camphor (public summaries)
EU CosIng / Cosmetic Regulation UV-filter annexes (public)

entries.title: Cyclohexasiloxane (D6)
entries.why: Cyclic silicone (D6) used for slip and feel, alongside D4/D5. EU environmental restrictions target cyclic siloxanes for persistence/bioaccumulation concerns rather than acute human toxicity at cosmetic levels.
sources: EU REACH restrictions on D4/D5/D6 cyclic siloxanes (public)
ECHA substance information on D6 (public summaries)

entries.title: Sodium laureth sulfate (SLES)
entries.why: Milder foaming surfactant than SLS, widely used in shampoos and body wash. Can still dry or irritate some users; ethoxylation may leave trace 1,4-dioxane impurities controlled by good manufacturing practice. Low severity irritation nuance.
sources: EU CosIng entry for sodium laureth sulfate (public)
SCCS/public reviews of alkyl ether sulfates as irritants (summaries)

entries.title: PEG compounds
entries.why: Polyethylene glycol derivatives act as emulsifiers, solubilisers, and texture agents. Generally low concern at cosmetic use levels; ethoxylation can introduce trace 1,4-dioxane if purification is poor—quality control, not an inherent active risk. Balanced low severity.
sources: EU CosIng entries for PEG derivatives (public)
Public regulatory notes on 1,4-dioxane as an impurity in ethoxylated ingredients

entries.title: Dimethicone
entries.why: Linear silicone polymer used for smooth feel, spread, and light water resistance. Not the same as restricted cyclic D4/D5/D6; generally considered low human-health concern at cosmetic use. Included for transparency, not alarm.
sources: EU CosIng entry for dimethicone (public)
SCCS/public silicone safety summaries where available

entries.title: EDTA (chelating salts)
entries.why: Chelating agent that binds metal ions to stabilise formulas and boost preservatives. Low direct skin toxicity at cosmetic levels; environmental persistence of free EDTA is the more common public discussion point. Mild transparency flag.
sources: EU CosIng entries for disodium EDTA and related salts (public)
Public environmental assessments of EDTA (summaries)

entries.title: Salicylic acid
entries.why: BHA used for exfoliation, acne care, and as a preservative aid. SCCS opinions set concentration limits and restrict use on children; can irritate and is not for unrestricted use in leave-on products. Informed-use moderate-low severity.
sources: SCCS opinion on salicylic acid (public summary)
EU Cosmetic Regulation Annex III — salicylic acid limits

entries.title: Acrylates (nail/film formers)
entries.why: Acrylic monomers and polymers used in nail enhancements, gels, and some film-forming cosmetics. Cured polymers are usually low concern; residual monomers can sensitise (classic salon acrylate allergy). Severity is for monomer/sensitisation context, not cured plastic.
sources: EU CosIng entries for acrylate monomers/polymers (public)
SCCS/public reviews of acrylate sensitisation in nail products (summaries)

entries.title: Toluene
entries.why: Aromatic solvent historically used in nail polish and removers for smooth application. Volatile and neurotoxicity concerns at high inhalation exposure; largely phased out of many modern formulas but still worth flagging when listed. Moderate severity for nail-product solvent use.
sources: EU CosIng entry for toluene (public)
Public occupational/solvent exposure summaries (regulatory context)

entries.title: Camphor
entries.why: Used in nail products for plasticity and as a fragrance/cooling note in some formulas. EU Annex III sets maximum concentrations; can irritate and is toxic if ingested in quantity. Low–moderate label note for nail and scented products.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — camphor
EU CosIng entry for camphor (public)

entries.title: Propylene glycol
entries.why: Humectant and solvent that helps dissolve actives and retain moisture. Generally low concern at cosmetic levels; can irritate or sensitise a minority of users at higher concentrations. Transparency flag only.
sources: EU CosIng entry for propylene glycol (public)
SCCS/public safety assessments of propylene glycol (summaries)

entries.title: Witch hazel (Hamamelis virginiana)
entries.why: Botanical astringent extract used in toners and aftershaves. Generally mild, but plant extracts and residual fragrance/tannin components can irritate or sensitise some users—especially alcohol-rich distillates. Low severity botanical note.
sources: EU CosIng entry for Hamamelis virginiana extracts (public)
SCCS botanical/contact allergy context for plant extracts (public summaries)

entries.title: Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia)
entries.why: Essential oil used for scent and antimicrobial marketing claims. Known contact allergen and irritant when undiluted or oxidised; SCCS and public dermatology sources caution against neat use. Moderate-low severity for sensitisation risk.
sources: SCCS opinion on tea tree oil (public summary)
EU CosIng entry for Melaleuca alternifolia leaf oil (public)

entries.title: Methylparaben
entries.why: Short-chain paraben preservative, among the most common and generally lower-concern members of the family versus butyl/propyl parabens under SCCS assessments. Still flagged for users who prefer to minimise all parabens.
sources: SCCS opinions on parabens (public summaries)
EU CosIng entry for methylparaben (public)

entries.title: Ethylparaben
entries.why: Short-chain paraben preservative with a more favourable SCCS profile than longer-chain butyl/propyl parabens. Low–moderate severity for people tracking preservatives rather than a high-priority ban signal.
sources: SCCS opinions on parabens (public summaries)
EU CosIng entry for ethylparaben (public)

entries.title: Iodopropynyl butylcarbamate (IPBC)
entries.why: Iodine-containing preservative effective against fungi. EU Annex III limits concentration and restricts use in leave-on products for children and on large body areas; can sensitise. Moderate severity restricted preservative.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 Annex III — IPBC
SCCS opinions on iodopropynyl butylcarbamate (public summaries)

entries.title: Alcohol denat.
entries.why: Denatured ethanol used as solvent, astringent, and texture aid in toners, sprays, and fragrances. Can dry or irritate skin when high on the list; not a CMR or banned concern. Low severity irritation nuance.
sources: EU CosIng entry for alcohol denat. (public)
Public dermatology summaries on ethanol as a skin irritant in leave-on cosmetics

entries.title: Petrolatum
entries.why: Occlusive mineral emollient that protects and softens skin. Cosmetic grades should meet purity (PAH) specifications under EU rules; refined petrolatum is generally low concern. Transparency flag for mineral-oil avoiders, not a hazard alarm.
sources: EU CosIng entry for petrolatum (public)
EU Cosmetic Regulation purity requirements for hydrocarbon waxes (public)

entries.title: Diethanolamine (DEA)
entries.why: Alkanolamine used historically as a pH adjuster and in surfactant systems. Restricted in cosmetics because of nitrosamine formation risk with certain ingredients; free DEA is limited under EU rules. Moderate severity.
sources: EU Cosmetic Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 — secondary amine / nitrosamine restrictions
EU CosIng entry for diethanolamine (public)
